sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, in the previous lesson we analyzed primary versus secondary data sources. Today we are talking about acquisition instruments—specifically surveys and web scraping. Aren't those completely different worlds? One asks people questions, and the other writes automated Python scripts to pull HTML!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: They seem opposite on the surface, Kaito, but from an engineering perspective they represent the two sides of data acquisition: Active Structured Inquiry versus Passive Automated Extraction. Both suffer from massive selection biases if you treat the raw captured sample as the truth.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: In surveys, if only twenty percent of people respond, the respondents might be completely unrepresentative of the population. And in web scraping, if target sites change their HTML or block our IP, our extraction pipeline collapses silently!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly. Today we will master the mathematical foundations to solve both: Inverse Propensity Weighting to debias surveys mathematically, and RFC 9309 politeness throttling and Jaccard structural drift detection to make web crawling resilient.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the flowchart in Slide 2. In surveys, we design clean questions, but attrition hits us in the red box. And in scraping, we start with robots.txt in amber, but then we have to handle DOM mutations in green. Is attrition mathematically equivalent to missing data?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Yes, precisely! Survey non-response is a missing data problem where the missingness mechanism is often informative. If satisfied customers take the survey and frustrated customers ignore it, the respondent sample is truncated.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And on the web scraping side, we see robots.txt audit leading to DOM parsing. Many junior developers jump straight to writing BeautifulSoup code without checking robots.txt or considering crawl delays!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: That is an invitation to get your crawler IP banned or inflict an unintentional Denial of Service attack on the remote server. Let us now examine the formal mathematics of survey non-response.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, look at that formula: Bias equals one minus f sub r, times the difference between respondents and non-respondents. That means if the people who don't answer have the exact same distribution as the people who do answer, the bias is zero!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Brilliant observation, Kaito! That corresponds to Missing Completely at Random, or MCAR. If Y bar sub r equals Y bar sub nr, then the gap is zero, so even a five percent response rate would yield an unbiased mean.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: But in the real world, non-response is almost never MCAR! People with high incomes might refuse to report salary, or users who experienced software crashes might be more motivated to fill out an incident report.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Precisely. The latent gap is virtually always non-zero. And because we do not directly observe Y bar sub nr for the dropouts, computing this bias requires auxiliary covariates and propensity modeling, which brings us to Inverse Propensity Weighting.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: So if an underrepresented demographic cohort only has a five percent chance of answering the survey, their propensity pi is 0.05. That means their weight w is one over 0.05, which equals twenty!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly, Kaito! Each respondent from that underrepresented cohort speaks on behalf of twenty individuals in the population. Conversely, someone from an overrepresented group with a propensity of 0.80 gets a weight of only 1.25.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: That's elegant! But what happens if someone has a tiny propensity, like 0.001? Their weight would explode to one thousand!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: You've hit on the greatest vulnerability of IPW: extreme weight inflation. Let's look at Slide 5 to see how we stabilize weights in production.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: So clipping the propensities between 0.05 and 0.95 caps our maximum weight at twenty! That trades a tiny amount of theoretical asymptotic bias for a massive reduction in variance.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Precisely. The classic bias-variance trade-off in action. In finite samples, an unbiased estimator with infinite variance is useless in production engineering.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Can we test this live? I want to see how changing the response rate and respondent mean changes the non-response bias and how IPW corrects it!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Right on cue, Kaito! Let us move down to our first interactive lab: The Survey Non-Response and IPW Debiasing Workbench.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, our speaker stage has traveled right down to the Survey Non-Response Simulator! Look at the four sliders: Population Universe, Response Rate, Respondent Mean, and Non-Respondent Mean.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Try setting Response Rate to twenty percent, Respondent Mean to 85, and Non-Respondent Mean to 45. Notice how the unweighted respondent mean overstates the true population mean by over thirty points! Try adjusting the controls now.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Ten thousand users surveyed, twenty percent response rate. The respondents gave an average score of 8.5, but the phone audit showed the silent non-respondents averaged only 4.5! That's a massive four-point gap!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Let us challenge our engineers: Use Groves' formula to calculate the exact true population mean Y bar and the resulting non-response bias. Select Option A, B, or C above us!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, I see people writing scraping scripts that fire fifty concurrent requests per second using asyncio without any crawl delay. That's why server administrators set up Cloudflare Turnstile and rate limits!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly, Kaito. Fifty requests per second on a small university or municipal website will overwhelm their database. If a robots.txt specifies Crawl-delay 0.5, your maximum throughput across all threads combined is strictly two requests per second.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And putting a real User-Agent with a project URL or email is huge. That way, if your scraper misbehaves, the administrator can email you instead of immediately banning your entire organization's subnet!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Well said. Now once our polite request arrives and we receive the HTML document, how do we parse it without writing fragile code? Let's analyze DOM tree traversal on Slide 9.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: I've definitely been guilty of copying XPath from Chrome DevTools! It gives you slash html slash body slash div bracket two, and it works great until the marketing team pushes a holiday banner, and suddenly div bracket two becomes div bracket three!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: And the catastrophic part is that the scraper doesn't crash with an exception—it simply returns an empty string or null! Your dataset quietly accumulates twenty thousand missing price values before anyone notices.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: That's silent data corruption! Using data-testid or schema.org JSON-LD tags keeps you insulated from UI tweaks because developers rarely change underlying test IDs.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly. But what happens if the target website undergoes a total redesign? That brings us to automated Structural Drift Detection using Jaccard distance on Slide 10.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Jaccard distance on DOM structural tokens! That's such a clever automated quality check. It compares the set of tags and classes on today's page with yesterday's page.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly. If an e-commerce website redesigns its catalog, the text of product titles might remain the same, but the surrounding container tags completely mutate. The Jaccard distance jumps to 0.50 or higher.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And by tripping a circuit breaker at 0.35, we prevent our automated pipeline from writing half a million empty or misaligned records into our feature store!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Precisely. Let us look at Slide 11 to see how all these pieces integrate into a complete production distributed scraping architecture.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: This architecture diagram ties everything together. Look at the content type routing branch: if the page is simple static HTML, it routes to a fast httpx worker. But if it requires client-side JavaScript execution, it routes to Playwright!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Exactly. Headless browsers consume massive memory and CPU resources. Running Chromium on every page is wasteful and slow; routing dynamically saves over eighty percent of infrastructure compute.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And before data ever reaches the Parquet lake, it must pass the Jaccard structural drift check in amber and MinHash deduplication in green! If it fails, it goes straight to the Dead-Letter Queue in red.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: That is the mark of enterprise engineering. Now, let us simulate rate limiting and structural drift live in our second interactive simulator!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, we have docked at the Web Scraping Simulator! Look at the three sliders: Crawl-delay, Concurrent Worker Threads, and DOM Tag Mutation Rate.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Try setting Crawl-delay to 0.5 seconds. The maximum allowable request rate is 2 requests per second. Now drag Concurrent Workers up to 8—watch the DoS warning badge flash red! Then increase DOM mutation rate past thirty-five percent to watch the circuit breaker trip.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Crawl-delay is set to 0.5 seconds. If you wait half a second between each request, how many requests can you send in one full second?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Let us see if our engineers remember the reciprocal relation: RPS max equals one over Crawl-delay. Select Option A, B, or C above us to verify!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Twenty-one percent response rate, and healthy people answered at over triple the rate of sick patients! If they had trained a machine learning model on raw survey respondents, it would have predicted that cardiovascular disease was nearly eradicated!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: A classic example of the healthy-user effect. Because they had scraped nationwide pharmacy prescription refills from public health portals, they had objective proof of how many prescriptions actually went unfilled.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: And by calibrating IPW weights against census age and income data, they wiped out ninety-four percent of the bias. Multi-modal synthesis at its finest!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Indeed. Now let us examine the complete, production-grade Python script that executes this IPW debiasing pipeline on Slide 15.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at line 18 in the Python code: np.clip propensities between 0.05 and 0.95! That prevents the weights from shooting up to infinity. And on line 25, np.average uses those weights to compute the debiased mean.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Notice how cleanly the assertions verify the mathematics: unweighted_bias must be over two thousand dollars because older people responded at higher rates. Then the second assertion proves that IPW suppresses residual bias to less than twenty percent of the original distortion.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Any engineer can copy this function directly into their data ingestion preprocessing pipeline and eliminate survey non-response distortion immediately!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: That is the power of combining statistical theory with software engineering. Now let us conclude with our Capstone Synthesis and the Four Golden Rules on Slide 16.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: What an incredible masterclass, Dr. Nova! We connected Groves' survey non-response theorem directly to Horvitz-Thompson IPW, and bridged that with RFC 9309 scraping politeness and Jaccard DOM drift detection.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: The common thread across all acquisition instruments is humility: the raw captured sample is almost never the unconfounded ground truth. Rigorous instrumentation models the observation mechanism itself.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: I can't wait for Lesson 2.4 when we explore APIs—REST endpoints, GraphQL query optimizations, and real-time streaming webhooks!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Thank you, Kaito, and thank you to all our engineers. See you in Lesson 2.4!
